text: Joanna of Castile (6 November 1479 – 12 April 1555), known historically as Joanna the Mad (Spanish: Juana la Loca), was the nominal queen of Castile from 1504 and queen of Aragon from 1516 until her death in 1555. She was the daughter of Queen Isabella I of Castile and King Ferdinand II of Aragon, both members of the House of Trastámara. Born on 6 November 1479 in Toledo, she was the fourth but third surviving child and the second daughter. Joanna had a fair complexion, brown eyes, and hair between strawberry-blonde and auburn, similar to her mother and sister Catherine. Her siblings were Isabella, Queen of Portugal; John, Prince of Asturias; Maria, Queen of Portugal; and Catherine, Queen of England. Educated in canon and civil law, genealogy, heraldry, grammar, history, languages, mathematics, philosophy, reading, spelling, and writing, she studied classical authors such as Juvencus, Prudentius, Saint Ambrose, Saint Augustine, Saint Gregory, Saint Jerome, and Seneca. Her tutors included Dominican priest Andrés de Miranda, educator Beatriz Galindo, and her mother. She learned court etiquette, dancing, drawing, equestrian skills, music, and needle arts like embroidery, needlepoint, sewing, spinning, and weaving. She became fluent in Castilian, Leonese, Galician-Portuguese, Catalan, French, and Latin and was skilled in dancing and music, playing the clavichord, guitar, and monochord. In 1496, at age 16, she was betrothed to 18-year-old Philip of Austria, son of Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian I and Duchess Mary of Burgundy, as part of a Habsburg-Trastámara alliance to counter French influence. The proxy marriage took place in Valladolid in August 1496, and the formal marriage occurred on 20 October 1496 in Lier, north of present-day Brussels. Between 1498 and 1507, she gave birth to six children—two boys and four girls—all of whom became emperors or queens. The deaths of her brother John, the stillbirth of John’s daughter, her older sister Isabella, and Isabella’s son Miguel made Joanna the heir to the Castilian and Aragonese thrones. In 1502, the Castilian Cortes of Toro recognized her as heiress to the Castilian throne and Philip as her consort, and she was named Princess of Asturias. The Aragonese Cortes in Zaragoza swore allegiance to her as heiress, though Archbishop Alonso de Aragón stated the oath could only establish succession through a formal agreement. In 1502, Philip, Joanna, and their court traveled to Toledo for her to receive fealty from the Cortes as Princess of Asturias, a journey detailed by Antoon I van Lalaing. After returning to the Low Countries, a pregnant Joanna remained in Madrid, giving birth to Ferdinand, who later became Holy Roman Emperor as Ferdinand I. Upon her mother’s death in November 1504, Joanna became queen regnant of Castile, and her husband Philip became king jure uxoris in 1506, initiating Habsburg rule. Ferdinand II, her father, refused to accept this and claimed governance in her name, citing her illness, which the Cortes accepted, appointing him as guardian and administrator. Philip also minted coins in the name of "Philip and Joanna, King and Queen of Castile, Léon and Archdukes of Austria," prompting Ferdinand to marry Germaine de Foix, niece of Louis XII of France, in hopes of producing a son to inherit Aragon and possibly Castile. In the Low Countries, Joanna was confined, but on 24 August 1505, she was released when her father-in-law Maximilian visited, and she participated in public events where she acted like a wise, prudent queen, noted by the Venetian ambassador. Philip and Maximilian jousted under torchlight, with Maximilian advising that a monarch must be "una cosa medesima" (one and the same). After this, the couple reconciled somewhat, and Joanna firmly refused to act against her father when Philip sought support from Castilian nobles. Ferdinand’s remarriage strengthened support for Philip and Joanna, and in late 1505, they traveled to Castile. Before departure, Joanna forbade a ship with female attendants, fearing illicit relationships, an action that fueled propaganda against her. Their ships were wrecked on the English coast, and they were hosted by Henry, Prince of Wales (later Henry VIII), and Joanna’s sister Catherine of Aragon at Windsor Castle. They were unable to leave until 21 April, by which time civil war was looming. Philip considered landing in Andalusia to rally nobles against Ferdinand, but instead landed at A Coruña on 26 April, where the Castilian nobility abandoned Ferdinand en masse. At Villafáfila on 27 June 1506, Ferdinand met Philip privately and unexpectedly handed over Castile’s government to his "most beloved children," promising to retire to Aragon. Philip and Ferdinand signed the Treaty of Villafáfila, agreeing that Joanna’s "infirmities and sufferings" made her incapable of ruling and that she would be excluded from government. Ferdinand repudiated this agreement the same afternoon, declaring that Joanna should never be deprived of her rights as Queen Proprietress of Castile. A fortnight later, without a new agreement, he abandoned Castile for Aragon, leaving Philip to govern in Joanna’s stead. On 9 July 1506, the procurators of the Cortes met in Valladolid and swore allegiance to Philip I and Joanna as King and Queen of Castile and León and to their son Charles as heir-apparent. This arrangement lasted only a few months. On 25 September 1506, Philip died in Burgos after a five-day illness, likely from typhoid fever, with rumors that Ferdinand II had poisoned him. Joanna was pregnant with their sixth child, a daughter named Catherine (1507–1578), who later became Queen of Portugal. Without a midwife, she was assisted by her lady-in-waiting, María de Ulloa. By 20 December 1506, Joanna was in Torquemada attempting to rule alone as Queen of Castile, but the country fell into disorder. Her son Charles, then six years old, was raised in Flanders by his aunt, and Ferdinand remained in Aragon. A regency council under Archbishop Cisneros was formed against her orders but failed to manage public disorder; plague and famine devastated the kingdom, killing half the population. Ferdinand returned to Castile in July 1507, coinciding with a remission of the plague and famine, which calmed instability and created the impression that his return restored the kingdom’s health. At Hornillos on 30 July 1507, Ferdinand constrained Joanna to yield power over Castile and León to himself. On 17 August 1507, three members of the royal council were summoned—supposedly in her name—and ordered to inform the grandees of Ferdinand’s return, stating they should serve him as they would her person and more. However, Joanna refused to sign the instructions and issued a statement asserting that as queen regnant she did not endorse the surrender of her royal powers. Despite this, she became queen in name only, with all official documents signed by Ferdinand as "I the King." In 1510, the Cortes of Castile named Ferdinand administrator of the kingdom and entrusted governance mainly to Archbishop Cisneros. In February 1509, Ferdinand confined Joanna in the Royal Palace in Tordesillas, near Valladolid, dismissing her faithful servants and appointing a small retinue under his control. At this time, some accounts claimed she was insane or "mad," and she reportedly took her husband’s corpse with her to Tordesillas. Upon the death of her father Ferdinand II on 23 January 1516, Joanna became Queen of Aragon. Cisneros and the regency council concealed the news, pretending Ferdinand still lived and ruled. Her 17-year-old son Charles arrived in Asturias at the Bay of Biscay in October 1517. Until his arrival, the Crown of Aragon was governed by Archbishop Alonso de Aragón (an illegitimate son of Ferdinand) and the Crown of Castile by Cardinal Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros. On 4 November, Charles and his sister Eleanor met Joanna at Tordesillas, where they secured her authorization for Charles to rule as co-King of Castile and León and of Aragon. Despite her acquiescence, her confinement continued, and Charles expanded deceptions, later hiding the 1519 death of Emperor Maximilian from her. The Castilian Cortes, meeting in Valladolid, addressed Charles only as Su Alteza ("Your Highness") and reserved Majestad ("Majesty") for Joanna, though no one seriously considered Joanna’s rule realistic. In 1519, Charles I ruled the Crown of Aragon and its territories and the Crown of Castile and its territories in personal union, and was elected Holy Roman Emperor. The kingdoms of Castile and Aragon (and Navarre) remained in personal union until their jurisdictional unification in the early 18th century by the Nueva Planta decrees. Charles eventually abdicated as Holy Roman Emperor in favor of his brother Ferdinand and as King of Spain in favor of his son Philip, marking the "transition from a universal empire to defence of the interests of the 'Austrian family' (austriacismo), in other words, to a close alliance between two parts of the dynasty, aimed at guaranteeing the hegemony of Catholicism and of the dynasty within Europe." In 1520, the Revolt of the Comuneros broke out in response to perceived foreign Habsburg influence through Charles V. The rebels demanded Castile be governed according to the practices of the Catholic Monarchs and turned to Joanna, as sovereign monarch, to legitimize their rebellion. To prevent this, Bishop Don Antonio de Rojas Manrique led a delegation to Tordesillas, asking Joanna to sign a document denouncing the Comuneros. She refused, requesting specific provisions. Before this could happen, the Comuneros stormed the virtually undefended city and requested her support. This prompted Adrian of Utrecht, the regent appointed by Charles V, to declare that Charles would lose Castile if she granted support. Though sympathetic to the rebels, she was persuaded by Ochoa de Landa and her confessor Fray John of Ávila that supporting the revolt would irreparably damage the country and her son’s kingship, so she refused to sign. The Battle of Villalar confirmed Charles’s victory over the revolt. Charles ensured his dominance by having his mother confined for the rest of her life in the now-demolished Royal Palace in Tordesillas, Castile. Joanna’s condition deteriorated further; she reportedly believed some nuns wanted to kill her and had difficulty eating, sleeping, bathing, or changing clothes. Charles wrote to her caretakers: "It seems to me that the best and most suitable thing for you to do is to make sure that no person speaks with Her Majesty."

This request prompted Adrian of Utrecht, the regent appointed by Charles V, to declare that Charles would lose Castile if she granted her support. Although she was sympathetic to the Comuneros, she was persuaded by Ochoa de Landa and her confessor Fray John of Ávila that supporting the revolt would irreparably damage the country and her son's kingship, and she therefore refused to sign a document granting her support. The Battle of Villalar confirmed that Charles would prevail over the revolt. Charles ensured his domination and throne by having his mother confined for the rest of her life in the now-demolished Royal Palace in Tordesillas, Castile. Joanna's condition degenerated further; she apparently became convinced that some of the nuns who cared for her wanted to kill her, and it was reportedly difficult for her to eat, sleep, bathe, or change her clothes. Charles wrote to her caretakers: "It seems to me that the best and most suitable thing for you to do is to make sure that no person speaks with Her Majesty, for no good could come from it." Her late mother's lady-in-waiting, Catalina de Medrano y Bravo de Lagunas, along with her husband, Hernando de Sandoval y Rojas, took part in the custody and care of Joanna in Tordesillas. Joanna also had her youngest daughter, Catherine of Austria, with her during Ferdinand II's time as regent, 1507–1516. Her older daughter, Eleanor of Austria, had created a semblance of a household within the palace rooms. In her final years, Joanna's physical state began to decline rapidly, with mobility ever more difficult. Joanna died on Good Friday, 12 April 1555, at the age of 75 in the Royal Palace at Tordesillas. She is entombed in the Royal Chapel of Granada in Spain, alongside her parents, Isabella I and Ferdinand II, her husband Philip I, and her nephew Miguel da Paz, Prince of Asturias. As a young woman, Joanna was known to be highly intelligent. Claims regarding her as "mad" are widely disputed. It was only after her marriage that the first suspicions of mental illness arose. Some historians believe she may have had melancholia, a depressive disorder, a psychosis, or a case of inherited schizophrenia. She may also have been unjustly painted as "mad" as her husband Philip the Handsome and her father, Ferdinand, had a great deal to gain from Joanna being declared sick or incompetent to rule. The narrative of her purported mental illness is perpetuated in stories of the mental illness of her maternal grandmother, Isabella of Portugal, Queen of Castile, who, in widowhood, was exiled by her stepson to the castle of Arévalo in Ávila, Castile. Bethany Aram argues that while she seemed to be unable or unwilling to rule herself, Joanna's major (political) significance lay with her defense of the rights of her descendants and thus the Habsburg dynasty. While she did have affection for Philip, her refusal to bury her husband (and attempt to bring his corpse to Granada so that he would lie beside her mother) was likely an attempt to ward off suitors and create a connection between Charles and Castile. Facing the leaders of the Comunero Revolt, she again chose the Habsburg dynasty over her Castilian heritage. Her fecundity provided Charles with many Habsburg siblings (and by extensions, these siblings' children) who upheld his rule. Sara T. Nalle agrees with Aram that this was Joanna's major success, while pointing out that Aram seems to gloss over the fact that Joanna's contemporaries did see her as different. Nalle opines that overall, Joanna was a troubled individual who, not trained for the political world, found herself surrounded by strong personalities, and had to face a shocking amount of cruelty and deceit.
